title: John 4:43–54
context: After two days Jesus goes to Galilee, where a prophet lacks hometown honor, yet Galileans welcome Him for feast-signs. At Cana an official from Capernaum begs Him to come down before his son dies. Jesus rebukes sign-hunger, then speaks: “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believes the word, meets servants on the road, matches the hour, and he and his household believe. This is the second sign from Judea to Galilee.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about believing the spoken word without first seeing the sign.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe. Go, thy son liveth. The man believed the word that Jesus spake—and that even without a miracle. And himself believed, and his whole house.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 4:48, 50, 53)

reformed.quote: He reproves them for being so eager for miracles… The nobleman believed the word of Christ, and went away. Faith comes by hearing. Afterwards he and his whole house believed: the first faith was not small, but it was increased and confirmed by the event.

verses.text: After the two days he went out from there and went into Galilee.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Samaritan stay ends on the original itinerary. Two days were enough to plant a confession and still leave.

Remaining and departing can both be obedience. The Savior of the world does not settle as Samaria’s chaplain only.
verses.reformedNotes:
After the two days: He keeps the Father’s clock.

The same necessity that brought Him through Samaria now sends Him on. Harvest there does not void the next appointment.

verses.text: For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.
verses.arminianNotes:
John explains Galilee with a proverb Jesus had used. Home is not always the easiest field.

Familiarity can starve honor. The proverb prepares us not to confuse a welcome (v. 45) with the faith of Samaria.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator cites Jesus’ own testimony. Hometown dishonor is expected, not accidental.

Galilee will welcome signs and still need a rebuke (v. 48). Honor and faith are not the same.

verses.text: So when he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem at the feast, for they also went to the feast.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Galileans welcome him because of the signs at the feast. They had gone up; they had seen; they receive Him as a wonder-worker returning.

Welcome is better than scorn and still may be sign-deep. John has already shown (2:23–25) that feast-faith can be something Jesus does not entrust Himself to.
verses.reformedNotes:
Having seen all the things that he had done: the ground of the welcome is miracles at the feast.

This is not yet the household faith of v. 53. Galilee’s smile is sight-born; the official will be called to word-born trust.

verses.text: Jesus came therefore again to Cana of Galilee, where he made the water into wine. There was a certain nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum.
verses.arminianNotes:
An official from Capernaum has a sick son—need traveling uphill to the sign-town.

Status does not exempt from fever. A royal official will have to ask like the Samaritan woman did: without leverage.
verses.reformedNotes:
Cana recalled, Capernaum introduced. Illness in a powerful house.

The second sign will answer a father’s desperation in the place of the first sign, teaching that the Giver, not the venue, is the point.

verses.text: When he heard that Jesus had come out of Judea into Galilee, he went to him and begged him that he would come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hearing, going, asking: come down before death. The prayer is specific and geographically small—Jesus must travel to the boy.

This is faith beginning, mixed with a theory of how Jesus has to work. Grace will honor the ask and correct the theory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Heard, went, asked: the man is not proud enough to stay in Capernaum. Point of death is the clock.

Desperation is often God’s doorway. The request still tries to manage the method: come down.

verses.text: Jesus therefore said to him, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Plural you: Galilee’s sign-habit, not only this father. Wesley heard a rebuke of dependence on wonders. Belief that requires a show is the feast-welcome’s underside.

Wesleyan Arminians take the warning as addressable. They can believe the word; Jesus is calling them off a demand that makes faith hostage to spectacle, while still about to give a sign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: He reproves eagerness for miracles. Unless you see—plural unbelief diagnosed.

Signs can become the price we charge God for trust. The official’s panic is folded into a people’s hunger for wonders; both need a better ground than sight.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear a rebuke of sign-conditioned faith. Arminians typically treat it as an earnest summons to trust the word now; Reformed readers commonly treat it as exposing a heart that will not believe unless God pays in wonders—and as the backdrop for faith that must be given.

verses.text: The nobleman said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He does not debate the rebuke; he pleads the child. Sir, come down—still method, more urgency.

Sometimes the holiest reply to a hard word is to keep asking for the dying. Jesus can fix the man’s theology after He hears the father’s voice.
verses.reformedNotes:
No apology tour: just the boy. Come down before he dies—faith and unbelief tangled in one sentence.

The Lord let the plea stand. He will not come down, and He will still meet the dying.

verses.text: Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.
verses.arminianNotes:
Go; your son will live. Wesley: he believed the word even without a miracle, and went. The sign is promised, not yet seen; the going is the faith.

Arminians linger on believed the word. Trust here is a response to a spoken promise—enabled, responsible, mobile. He does not stay to negotiate a house-call.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the nobleman believed the word and went away; faith comes by hearing. The life of the boy is in a sentence.

Jesus refuses the trip and gives a promise. The man’s going is created by that word. Hearing, not seeing, is the appointed instrument.
verses.keyContrast: Both agree: he believes the spoken word and goes before any proof. Arminians typically describe that believing as a grace-enabled, uncoerced trust in the promise. Reformed readers typically describe the same moment as faith coming by hearing—the word itself effecting the trust it commands.

verses.text: As he was going down, his servants met him and reported, saying “Your child lives!”
verses.arminianNotes:
On the road, confirmation meets obedience. Recovering: the promise is already in progress.

Going is not a leap into silence. The God who speaks also sends servants with news; faith is often met midway.
verses.reformedNotes:
Going down, met, told: providence uses household staff.

The recovery is underway while the father is still traveling on the word. The sign catches up with faith, not the reverse.

verses.text: So he inquired of them the hour when he began to get better. They said therefore to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He checks the hour—not unbelief so much as wanting the word and the event to kiss. Seventh hour: yesterday, one p.m., fever gone.

Faith may still ask when. Matching clocks is allowed; it will become worship in v. 53, not a demand for a third sign.
verses.reformedNotes:
The hour is investigated and named. Fever left: sudden, datable.

God lets the miracle be timestamped so the word’s authority is unmistakable. This is not vague improvement; it is the seventh hour.

verses.text: So the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus said to him, “Your son lives.” He believed, as did his whole house.
verses.arminianNotes:
He knew the hours matched. He believed, as did his household—Wesley notes the house with him. The first believing (v. 50) deepens into a household confession.

One man’s trust becomes a home’s trust without erasing anyone’s hearing. The word that saved a boy now names a family as believers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the first faith was not small, but increased and confirmed by the event; then he and his whole house believed.

Sign serves word, then spreads. Household faith is the overflow of a promise God kept at the hour He spoke it.
verses.keyContrast: Both see two stages: believing the word on the road, then a confirmed, household faith. Arminians typically describe the increase as further free response to clearer light. Reformed readers describe it as the same divine word confirming and extending the faith it first created.

verses.text: This is again the second sign that Jesus did, having come out of Judea into Galilee.
verses.arminianNotes:
John numbers it: second sign, Judea-to-Galilee. Cana’s wine and a Capernaum fever bookend a journey through Samaria’s well.

Signs are true and ordered, never the master. The chapter that offered living water ends with a boy alive because a father believed a sentence. That is the kind of seeing John wants.
verses.reformedNotes:
John tags the second sign with its location. John the narrator keeps the score so we will not miss the pattern.

Signs certify the Speaker of 4:50. Galilee gets a wonder, Samaria got two days of word, and both are the same Christ gathering believers as He will.
